import numpy as np
from PIL import Image

img = np.asarray(Image.open('barcode.png').convert('RGB')).astype(float)
h, w, _ = img.shape
cols = img.mean(axis=0)
lum = 0.2126*cols[:,0] + 0.7152*cols[:,1] + 0.0722*cols[:,2]
sat = cols.max(axis=1) - cols.min(axis=1)

# Find the orange region: R much greater than B
orange = (cols[:,0] - cols[:,1] > 15) & (cols[:,1] - cols[:,2] > 5)
idx = np.where(orange)[0]
if len(idx):
    # group contiguous
    groups = np.split(idx, np.where(np.diff(idx) > 5)[0]+1)
    print("Orange groups (start%, width, mean RGB):")
    for g in groups:
        if len(g) >= 3:
            r,gg,b = cols[g].mean(axis=0)
            print(f"  x={g[0]}-{g[-1]} ({g[0]/10:.1f}%-{g[-1]/10:.1f}%, width {len(g)}): RGB=({r:.0f},{gg:.0f},{b:.0f})")

# Bright bands (lum > 60)
bright = np.where(lum > 60)[0]
if len(bright):
    groups = np.split(bright, np.where(np.diff(bright) > 5)[0]+1)
    print("\nBright bands (lum>60):")
    for g in groups:
        if len(g) >= 3:
            r,gg,b = cols[g].mean(axis=0)
            print(f"  x={g[0]}-{g[-1]} ({g[0]/10:.1f}%-{g[-1]/10:.1f}%, width {len(g)}): RGB=({r:.0f},{gg:.0f},{b:.0f})")

# First and last 10 columns
print("\nFirst 10 cols mean RGB:", cols[:10].mean(axis=0).round(0))
print("Last 10 cols mean RGB:", cols[-10:].mean(axis=0).round(0))

# Warm vs cool tendency over time (R-B difference), 50 buckets
print("\n-- 50 buckets: pos%, lum, R-B (warmth), saturation --")
for i in range(50):
    a, b = i*w//50, (i+1)*w//50
    L = lum[a:b].mean(); rb = (cols[a:b,0]-cols[a:b,2]).mean(); s = sat[a:b].mean()
    bar = '#' * int(L/3)
    print(f"{i*2:3d}-{(i+1)*2:3d}%: L={L:5.1f} warm={rb:+5.1f} sat={s:5.1f} {bar}")
EOF

***The Haunting in Connecticut*** is a 2009 [supernatural horror film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernatural_horror_film "Supernatural horror film") directed by [Peter Cornwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Cornwell_\(director\) "Peter Cornwell (director)") in his feature directorial debut,[\[8\]](#cite_note-9) and starring [Virginia Madsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Madsen "Virginia Madsen"), [Kyle Gallner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyle_Gallner "Kyle Gallner"), [Martin Donovan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Donovan "Martin Donovan"), [Amanda Crew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Crew "Amanda Crew"), and [Elias Koteas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elias_Koteas "Elias Koteas"). The film follows a family who, to help mitigate the strains of travel on their cancer-stricken son, move into a former [funeral home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funeral_home "Funeral home") with a dark history. It is based on the alleged supernatural experiences of Carmen Snedeker and her family while residing in a former funeral home in [Southington, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southington,_Connecticut "Southington, Connecticut") in the late 1980s. The Snedeker family's experiences were documented by writer [Ray Garton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Garton "Ray Garton") in *In a Dark Place: The Story of a True Haunting* (1992), though Garton later publicly distanced himself from the accuracy of the events he depicted in the book.[\[9\]](#cite_note-10)[\[10\]](#cite_note-11)

Development of *The Haunting in Connecticut* began in 2007 through [Gold Circle Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Circle_Films "Gold Circle Films"), with [John Carpenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carpenter "John Carpenter") originally attached as director, though Carpenter eventually backed out of the project due to creative differences, with Cornwell serving as his replacement. Principal photography took place in [Teulon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teulon "Teulon"), Manitoba in late 2007\.

*The Haunting in Connecticut* had its world premiere at [South by Southwest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_by_Southwest "South by Southwest") in [Austin, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin,_Texas "Austin, Texas") on March 17, 2009, before being theatrically released in the United States and Canada the following week. The film grossed approximately $78.8 million internationally.[\[7\]](#cite_note-NUM-8) Critical reaction to the film was largely unfavorable, though it did receive some praise for its atmosphere, visual elements, and performances.[\[ii\]](#cite_note-reviews-17)

In 2010, Gold Circle Films announced the production of an indirect sequel, *[The Haunting in Connecticut 2: Ghosts of Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Haunting_in_Connecticut_2:_Ghosts_of_Georgia "The Haunting in Connecticut 2: Ghosts of Georgia")*,[\[16\]](#cite_note-variety.com-18) which was released in 2013\.

## Plot

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")\]

In 1987, Sara Campbell is driving her son Matt home from a [Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecticut "Connecticut") hospital where he has been undergoing [experimental cancer treatments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_cancer_treatment "Experimental cancer treatment"). Sara and her husband, Peter, a recovering alcoholic, discuss finding a rental house closer to the hospital. On another hospital visit, Sara finds a man putting up a "For Rent" sign in front of a large house. The man is frustrated and offers her the first month free if she rents the house immediately.

The following day, Peter arrives with Matt's brother Billy and cousins Wendy and Mary, and they choose rooms. Matt chooses the basement, which is divided by a [partition wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall#Partition_wall "Wall") with a locked door. After moving in, Matt suffers a series of [visions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vision_\(spirituality\) "Vision (spirituality)") involving an old, bearded man and corpses with symbols carved into their skin. The next day, Peter learns that the house was originally a [funeral home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funeral_home "Funeral home"); the room behind the mysterious door in the basement is a [mortuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgue "Morgue").

Matt tells another cancer patient, Reverend Nicholas Popescu, about his visions. Nicholas advises him to find out what the spirit wants. Later, Matt encounters a burned figure in his room who begins to move toward him. When the family comes home, they find a shirtless Matt with his fingers bleeding from scratching at the wall.

The family begins to disintegrate under the stress of Matt's illness and bizarre behavior. The children find a box of photographs, which show Jonah, a young man from Matt's visions, at a [séance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Séance "Séance"), emitting [ectoplasm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ectoplasm_\(paranormal\) "Ectoplasm (paranormal)") from his mouth. They also find a container of desiccated human [eyelids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyelid "Eyelid"). Wendy and Matt discover that the funeral home was run by a man named Ramsey Aickman, who conducted psychic research and would host séances with Jonah acting as a [medium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediumship "Mediumship"). At one séance, all those attending, including Aickman, were found dead, and Jonah disappeared.

Nicholas theorizes that Aickman was practicing [necromancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Necromancy "Necromancy") in an attempt to control the dead and bind them to the house. That night, Nicholas finds human remains in the house and removes them. Matt awakens to find Aickman's symbols carved into his skin. He is taken to the hospital, where he encounters Jonah's ghost. Nicholas and Matt begin to have simultaneous visions revealing Jonah's fate: During the séance, a demonic presence burnt all the attendees in a flash of light. Jonah fled, using a [dumbwaiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dumbwaiter "Dumbwaiter") to escape the basement, but inadvertently became trapped in the [crematory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crematory "Crematory"), where he was [cremated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cremation "Cremation") alive.

Peter and Sara learn that Matt's cancer treatments have had no effect. They then discover that Matt has escaped the hospital. At home, Nicholas leaves a message telling the family to get out immediately, as it was Jonah's spirit that protected them. Matt breaks through the walls in the front room with an axe, revealing the dusty corpses Aickman hid in the walls. He forces Wendy and the children outside before barricading himself in the house and tearing down the other walls as corpses begin to tumble into the room. Jonah seemingly [possesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirit_possession "Spirit possession") Matt, who lights the bodies and the room on fire. Later on, investigators arrive at the house only to find it engulfed in flames.

As the fire department arrives, Sara and Peter frantically try to get in to save Matt. The spirits, finally freed, disappear. Outside, everyone watches tearfully as the emergency crew attempts to revive a dying Matt. As Matt slips away, he experiences a vision of himself standing in the graveyard where he sees Jonah, no longer appearing burnt. He seems about to follow Jonah when he hears his mother's voice. Matt returns to his body, and Jonah's spirit leaves him.

An [intertitle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intertitle "Intertitle") reveals that after the events, Matt's cancer miraculously disappeared. The house was rebuilt and resold with no further reported incidents of haunting.

## Production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")\]

### Development

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Development")\]

The origins of *The Haunting in Connecticut* date back to 2003, when screenwriter and producer [Daniel Farrands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Farrands "Daniel Farrands") presented the story to producer [Andrew Trapani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Trapani "Andrew Trapani").[\[17\]](#cite_note-TwoDeadBoys-19)[\[18\]](#cite_note-20) The film's screenplay, by [Adam Simon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Simon "Adam Simon") and Tim Metcalfe, is based on the alleged supernatural experiences of Carmen Snedeker and her family, who moved into a former [Southington, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southington,_Connecticut "Southington, Connecticut") funeral home during her son Stephen's cancer treatments in 1986\.[\[19\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWetmore202132-21)[\[20\]](#cite_note-22) The Snedekers' experiences were documented in the 1992 book *In a Dark Place: The Story of a True Haunting* by [Ray Garton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Garton "Ray Garton").[\[19\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWetmore202132-21) Carmen Snedeker provided input to the screenwriters over the course of approximately two years while the screenplay was being drafted.[\[21\]](#cite_note-Morrow-23)

In early 2007, [Gold Circle Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Circle_Films "Gold Circle Films") was reportedly discussing a directing contract with [John Carpenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carpenter "John Carpenter") for *The Haunting in Connecticut*. Although Carpenter was initially interested, the deal quickly fell through due to creative differences. Carpenter did enjoy the film's concept and would later agree to direct *[The Ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ward_\(film\) "The Ward (film)")* due to its similarities in tone and theme with *The Haunting in Connecticut*.[\[22\]](#cite_note-24)

### Casting

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Casting")\]

Virginia Madsen was cast in the film in May 2007 as Sara Campbell, the matriarch of the family.[\[23\]](#cite_note-25) According to producer [Paul Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Brooks "Paul Brooks"), Madsen was the first actress sought for the role.[\[17\]](#cite_note-TwoDeadBoys-19) "Virginia had a great combination of warmth and authority," said director Cornwell, "and she really helped to sell the reality of the family’s experience."[\[24\]](#cite_note-StuffWeLike-26)

Madsen stated that she had been interested in making a horror film, and had recently read "about 25 scripts" that she felt gave her "nothing to do."[\[17\]](#cite_note-TwoDeadBoys-19) When the role was offered to her, Madsen responded positively to the screenplay and its elements of interpersonal family drama.[\[17\]](#cite_note-TwoDeadBoys-19) Commenting on her portrayal of a real person, Madsen said: "I think something life-changing happened to that family. I don't know how much of what happened would meet my definition of real. I don't know what happened to them—and I don't even know how much I believe. Then, of course, we took a little Hollywood license. In the end, I can only play what's in the script."[\[21\]](#cite_note-Morrow-23)

In September 2007, *[The Hollywood Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hollywood_Reporter "The Hollywood Reporter")* announced the casting of Kyle Gallner, Martin Donovan, and Elias Koteas.[\[25\]](#cite_note-27) The film reunited Madsen and Koteas, who had previously been co-stars in the horror film *[The Prophecy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Prophecy "The Prophecy")* (1995).[\[26\]](#cite_note-King-28)

### Filming

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Filming")\]

[Principal photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_photography "Principal photography") began on September 10, 2007, in [Teulon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teulon "Teulon") and [Winnipeg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winnipeg "Winnipeg"), Manitoba Canada,[\[27\]](#cite_note-29) and was completed after approximately two months.[\[21\]](#cite_note-Morrow-23) The majority of filming took place in a historic 101-year-old home in Teulon.[\[26\]](#cite_note-King-28)

The film features several historical photographs from the archives of [Thomas Glendenning Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Glendenning_Hamilton "Thomas Glendenning Hamilton"), a Canadian [spiritualist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritualism_\(movement\) "Spiritualism (movement)") who photographed numerous séances, depicting alleged incidents of ectoplasm and other supernatural phenomena.[\[28\]](#cite_note-30)

## Factual basis

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Factual basis")\]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Lorraine_Warren.jpg/250px-Lorraine_Warren.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lorraine_Warren.jpg)

[Lorraine Warren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_and_Lorraine_Warren "Ed and Lorraine Warren"), who investigated the alleged haunting depicted in the film, indicated the film was "very loosely based" on the actual investigation[\[29\]](#cite_note-Reel-31)

Promotional material for the film claimed that it was "based on true events" experienced by the Snedeker family of Southington, Connecticut, in 1986\.[\[30\]](#cite_note-Radford-32) Paranormal investigators [Ed and Lorraine Warren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_and_Lorraine_Warren "Ed and Lorraine Warren") claimed that the Snedeker house was a former funeral home where morticians regularly practiced [necromancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Necromancy "Necromancy") and engaged in [necrophilia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Necrophilia "Necrophilia"), and that there were "powerful" supernatural "forces at work" that were cured by an [exorcism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exorcism "Exorcism").[\[30\]](#cite_note-Radford-32)[\[29\]](#cite_note-Reel-31)[\[31\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrown20087-33) Carmen Snedeker's claims of haunting by an "evil entity" and subsequent exorcism were dramatized in episodes of the television series *[A Haunting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Haunting "A Haunting")* (2002),[\[32\]](#cite_note-34) *[Paranormal Witness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paranormal_Witness "Paranormal Witness")* (2012),[\[33\]](#cite_note-35) and *[Mysteries at the Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mysteries_at_the_Museum "Mysteries at the Museum")* (2014).[\[34\]](#cite_note-36)[\[35\]](#cite_note-37)

However, according to skeptical investigator [Benjamin Radford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Radford "Benjamin Radford"), there is "little or no proof that anything supernatural occurred at the house."[\[36\]](#cite_note-livescience.com-38) Radford wrote that author [Ray Garton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Garton "Ray Garton") was employed by the Warrens to write the supposedly "true story" and was instructed by Ed Warren, "You've got some of the story — just use what works and make the rest up… Just make it up and make it scary."[\[36\]](#cite_note-livescience.com-38)

Researcher [Joe Nickell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Nickell "Joe Nickell") has dismissed the story as a [hoax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoax "Hoax"),[\[37\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENickell2012286-39) and claimed that the Snedekers' landlady "found the whole story ridiculous," adding that no residents before or since had experienced anything unusual in the home.[\[36\]](#cite_note-livescience.com-38) The landlady also noted that, despite their claims of paranormal activity, the Snedekers continued to reside in the home for over two years before deciding to leave.[\[36\]](#cite_note-livescience.com-38) Nickell noted that since Ed Warren died in 2006, some of his coauthors have admitted he "told them to make up incidents and details to create scary stories."[\[37\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENickell2012286-39) In an interview prior to the film's release, Lorraine Warren commented:

> The movie is very, very loosely based on the actual investigation... It was back in the '80s. We were called, it was very late at night, that Ed and I were called by a woman and her niece who were living with her at the time... The boys were the first to start talking about things they had seen and experienced, saying they were terrified. The parents were kind of chastising the kids—they thought it was all crazy. But the kids were so scared they started sleeping on the floor in the living room. It finally got to the point where we contacted the bishop’s office in [Hartford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartford,_Connecticut "Hartford, Connecticut"). Thank God he was very open to our work and what was going on. He sent two priests to the house and both of these priests were very high in the church. One had been used as an exorcist. They came to the house and said mass.[\[29\]](#cite_note-Reel-31)

## Release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Release")\]

In October 2008, [MTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV "MTV") released the film's first official theatrical trailer.[\[38\]](#cite_note-40) The film was originally planned for a June 19, 2009 theatrical release,[\[39\]](#cite_note-41) but in February 2009, its distributor, [Lionsgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionsgate_Films "Lionsgate Films"), announced that the release had been moved to March of that year.[\[40\]](#cite_note-42)

*The Haunting in Connecticut* premiered at [South by Southwest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_by_Southwest "South by Southwest") in [Austin, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin,_Texas "Austin, Texas") on March 17, 2009\.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Leydon-1)[\[41\]](#cite_note-43) It was theatrically released in the United States and Canada ten days later, on March 27, 2009\.[\[42\]](#cite_note-44) Lionsgate handled distribution in the United States, while in Canada, the film was distributed by [Maple Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maple_Pictures "Maple Pictures").[\[43\]](#cite_note-45) Due to favorable [test screenings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Test_screening "Test screening"), Lionsgate increased the film's U.S. release platform from approximately 2,200 screens to over 2,700.[\[44\]](#cite_note-46)

The owners of the actual Southington, Connecticut home depicted in the film reported that the film's publicity had resulted in numerous individuals visiting and photographing the residence in the weeks leading up to its release.[\[45\]](#cite_note-47)

### Home media

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Home media")\]

*The Haunting in Connecticut* was released on [DVD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DVD "DVD") and [Blu-ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blu-ray "Blu-ray") on July 14, 2009, featuring an extended 102-minute cut of the film.[\[3\]](#cite_note-McGaughy-3)[\[46\]](#cite_note-Gingold-48)[\[47\]](#cite_note-49) It debuted in the number one position on the DVD and Blu-ray charts with 1\.5 million units sold.[\[48\]](#cite_note-50) [Rentrak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rentrak "Rentrak") reported that the DVD release of *The Haunting in Connecticut* was no. 1 in DVD sales for the week ending July 19, 2009\.[\[49\]](#cite_note-51)[\[50\]](#cite_note-52)[\[51\]](#cite_note-53)

The extended version DVD includes a commentary with director Peter Cornwell, co-writer Adam Simon, producer [Andrew Trapani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Trapani "Andrew Trapani"), and editor Tom Elkins, a second commentary with the director and actors Virginia Madsen and Kyle Gallner, [deleted scenes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deleted_scene "Deleted scene") with optional director commentary, featurettes ("Two Dead Boys: Making of The Haunting in Connecticut", "The Fear is Real: Re-Investigating the Haunting", "Memento Mori: The History of Post Mortem Photography", "Anatomy of a Haunting"), and a digital copy of the film on a second disc.[\[46\]](#cite_note-Gingold-48)

## Reception

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Reception")\]

### Box office

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Box office")\]

In North America, the film opened in second place (behind *[Monsters vs. Aliens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monsters_vs._Aliens "Monsters vs. Aliens")*), averaging $8,420 at 2,732 theatres and grossing $23,004,765.[\[6\]](#cite_note-BOM-7)[\[54\]](#cite_note-56) *[The Hollywood Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hollywood_Reporter "The Hollywood Reporter")* noted the film was a financial success, reporting in June 2009 that it was the 25th-most profitable film of the year at that time.[\[55\]](#cite_note-Zeitchik-57)

The film remained in distribution in 39 international markets through July 22, 2010\.[\[6\]](#cite_note-BOM-7) Its final North American gross was $55.4 million and it made a further $23.4 million internationally for a worldwide total of $78.8 million.[\[7\]](#cite_note-NUM-8) In 2012, the film was re-released in [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"), where it grossed an additional $41,961.[\[6\]](#cite_note-BOM-7)

### Critical response

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Critical response")\]

On the [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), 17% of 105 critics' reviews are positive, with an average rating of 4\.3/10. The website's consensus reads: "Though it features a few scares and some creepy atmosphere, *The Haunting in Connecticut* ultimately relies too much on familiar horror cliches to achieve its goals."[\[56\]](#cite_note-Rotten_Tomatoes-58) [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), which uses a [weighted average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_arithmetic_mean "Weighted arithmetic mean"), assigned the film a score of 33 out of 100, based on 23 critics, indicating "generally unfavorable" reviews.[\[57\]](#cite_note-Metacritic-59) Audiences polled by [CinemaScore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CinemaScore "CinemaScore") gave the film an average grade of "B−" on an A+ to F scale.[\[58\]](#cite_note-60) While the film was mainly criticized for its use of horror cliches and "jump" scare tactics,[\[59\]](#cite_note-61) certain aspects of the film were praised by many critics, including the atmosphere and performances.[\[ii\]](#cite_note-reviews-17)

Jeannette Catsoulis of *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* praised the film's "genuinely grisly imagery" but expressed dislike for its "screechy" musical score, summarizing: "Spinning another based-on-actual-events tale of a family ejected from its home by angry spirits, *The Haunting in Connecticut* gives you the creeps, the giggles and the groans in almost equal measure."[\[60\]](#cite_note-62) [Alonso Duralde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alonso_Duralde "Alonso Duralde") of *[Today](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Today_\(American_TV_program\) "Today (American TV program)")* found the film's use of jump scares "gimmicky," adding that he wished the film "had trusted its plot and its dank visuals—which are often extraordinary—instead of relying on cheap thrills of the cat-jumps-out-of-the-closet variety."[\[11\]](#cite_note-Duralde-12) Film critic [Roger Ebert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Ebert "Roger Ebert") said the film "is a technically proficient horror movie and well acted," though he gave the movie only two stars.[\[61\]](#cite_note-63) Writing for *[Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_\(magazine\) "Empire (magazine)")*, [Kim Newman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Newman "Kim Newman") awarded the film two out of five stars, writing: "There’s a germ of an idea in the terminally ill teen attuned to seeing ghosts because he’s almost one himself, but Gallner’s smothered by Madsen’s hand-wringing mom, Martin Donovan’s dad and smarmy Elias Koteas in an *[Exorcist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Exorcist "The Exorcist")* hat. It has gruesome touches (a box of snipped-off eyelids), but the sudden-grab scares soon get pretty tiresome."[\[62\]](#cite_note-64)

Jim Vejvoda of *[IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN "IGN")* found the film "effective" despite being formulaic, adding that it "has very human and relatable characters at its core—a family that was already in peril due to the terminal illness of a family member—that keeps the viewer engaged in the story even as things grow more fantastical."[\[12\]](#cite_note-Vejvoda-13) Katherine Monk of the *[Calgary Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calgary_Herald "Calgary Herald")* similarly praised the film's emotional core, writing: "Like all movies crafted in the twilight world between the dead and the living, *The Haunting in Connecticut* ramps up suspense by pulling these two dimensions as close together as possible—with Matt becoming the human junction point."[\[63\]](#cite_note-65)

[Joe Leydon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Leydon "Joe Leydon") of *[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_\(magazine\) "Variety (magazine)")* noted that director Cornwell "sets up the story with brisk efficiency and a reasonable degree of logic," but ultimately felt that "nothing here rises above the level of routine haunted-house bumping-in-the-night."[\[1\]](#cite_note-Leydon-1) Writing for the *[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times "Los Angeles Times")*, Mark Olsen observed that the film "seems most at ease when it is playing more like a domestic drama than a horror tale, with the rather unsettling implication early on that what is happening may be a hallucinatory side effect of the boy’s trial cancer treatments. But *Haunting* suffers for its need to be sold as a straight-up horror film, and the fact it has been seemingly retrofitted as such."[\[64\]](#cite_note-66)

Tim Robey of *[The Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Daily_Telegraph "The Daily Telegraph")* gave the film a favorable review, writing: "The movie's heebie-jeebie sound design errs on the side of shameless, but there's a strong emotional core here, and a pretty good script... This is the best \[haunted house film\] in quite a while."[\[13\]](#cite_note-Robey-14) Randall King of the *[Winnipeg Free Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winnipeg_Free_Press "Winnipeg Free Press")* praised the cast as "sufficiently skilled" and found the atmosphere and filming locations effective.[\[65\]](#cite_note-KingReview-67) Sara Schieron of *[Boxoffice Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxoffice_Pro "Boxoffice Pro")* awarded the film three out of five stars, summarizing: "For as flawed as it is, *Haunting* features too many good bits to disregard... For an odd little relic—or should I say throwback?—the film’s scary parts certainly stick to you. You may laugh at the dramatics but you’ll be afraid to turn the light off when you go to bed."[\[66\]](#cite_note-68)

## Sequel

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Sequel")\]

In June 2009, [Gold Circle Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Circle_Films "Gold Circle Films") announced the development of two unrelated sequels forming a film [trilogy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trilogy "Trilogy"), the first titled *A Haunting in New York*, based on another case profiled on the [Discovery Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_Channel "Discovery Channel") series *[A Haunting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Haunting "A Haunting")*.[\[69\]](#cite_note-Trilogy-71) The second planned sequel was entitled *A Haunting in Georgia*, based on the alleged supernatural experiences of a young girl in [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_\(U.S._state\) "Georgia (U.S. state)").[\[69\]](#cite_note-Trilogy-71)

While production of *A Haunting in New York* never materialized, Gold Circle Films produced a [spiritual successor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_successor "Spiritual successor") sequel, *[The Haunting in Connecticut 2: Ghosts of Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Haunting_in_Connecticut_2:_Ghosts_of_Georgia "The Haunting in Connecticut 2: Ghosts of Georgia")*.[\[55\]](#cite_note-Zeitchik-57) [Ti West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ti_West "Ti West") was originally attached to direct,[\[55\]](#cite_note-Zeitchik-57) though Tom Elkins was ultimately hired as director, with David Coggeshall as the screenwriter.[\[70\]](#cite_note-72)[\[71\]](#cite_note-73)[\[72\]](#cite_note-74) It was released in a limited theatrical run, and through [video on demand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_on_demand "Video on demand"), on February 1, 2013\.[\[73\]](#cite_note-75)

***The Haunting in Connecticut*** is a 2009 [supernatural horror film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernatural_horror_film "Supernatural horror film") directed by [Peter Cornwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Cornwell_\(director\) "Peter Cornwell (director)") in his feature directorial debut,[\[8\]](#cite_note-9) and starring [Virginia Madsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Madsen "Virginia Madsen"), [Kyle Gallner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyle_Gallner "Kyle Gallner"), [Martin Donovan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Donovan "Martin Donovan"), [Amanda Crew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Crew "Amanda Crew"), and [Elias Koteas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elias_Koteas "Elias Koteas"). The film follows a family who, to help mitigate the strains of travel on their cancer-stricken son, move into a former [funeral home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funeral_home "Funeral home") with a dark history. It is based on the alleged supernatural experiences of Carmen Snedeker and her family while residing in a former funeral home in [Southington, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southington,_Connecticut "Southington, Connecticut") in the late 1980s. The Snedeker family's experiences were documented by writer [Ray Garton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Garton "Ray Garton") in *In a Dark Place: The Story of a True Haunting* (1992), though Garton later publicly distanced himself from the accuracy of the events he depicted in the book.[\[9\]](#cite_note-10)[\[10\]](#cite_note-11)

Development of *The Haunting in Connecticut* began in 2007 through [Gold Circle Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Circle_Films "Gold Circle Films"), with [John Carpenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carpenter "John Carpenter") originally attached as director, though Carpenter eventually backed out of the project due to creative differences, with Cornwell serving as his replacement. Principal photography took place in [Teulon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teulon "Teulon"), Manitoba in late 2007\.

*The Haunting in Connecticut* had its world premiere at [South by Southwest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_by_Southwest "South by Southwest") in [Austin, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin,_Texas "Austin, Texas") on March 17, 2009, before being theatrically released in the United States and Canada the following week. The film grossed approximately $78.8 million internationally.[\[7\]](#cite_note-NUM-8) Critical reaction to the film was largely unfavorable, though it did receive some praise for its atmosphere, visual elements, and performances.[\[ii\]](#cite_note-reviews-17)

In 2010, Gold Circle Films announced the production of an indirect sequel, *[The Haunting in Connecticut 2: Ghosts of Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Haunting_in_Connecticut_2:_Ghosts_of_Georgia "The Haunting in Connecticut 2: Ghosts of Georgia")*,[\[16\]](#cite_note-variety.com-18) which was released in 2013\.

## Plot

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")\]

In 1987, Sara Campbell is driving her son Matt home from a [Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecticut "Connecticut") hospital where he has been undergoing [experimental cancer treatments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_cancer_treatment "Experimental cancer treatment"). Sara and her husband, Peter, a recovering alcoholic, discuss finding a rental house closer to the hospital. On another hospital visit, Sara finds a man putting up a "For Rent" sign in front of a large house. The man is frustrated and offers her the first month free if she rents the house immediately.

The following day, Peter arrives with Matt's brother Billy and cousins Wendy and Mary, and they choose rooms. Matt chooses the basement, which is divided by a [partition wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall#Partition_wall "Wall") with a locked door. After moving in, Matt suffers a series of [visions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vision_\(spirituality\) "Vision (spirituality)") involving an old, bearded man and corpses with symbols carved into their skin. The next day, Peter learns that the house was originally a [funeral home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funeral_home "Funeral home"); the room behind the mysterious door in the basement is a [mortuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgue "Morgue").

Matt tells another cancer patient, Reverend Nicholas Popescu, about his visions. Nicholas advises him to find out what the spirit wants. Later, Matt encounters a burned figure in his room who begins to move toward him. When the family comes home, they find a shirtless Matt with his fingers bleeding from scratching at the wall.

The family begins to disintegrate under the stress of Matt's illness and bizarre behavior. The children find a box of photographs, which show Jonah, a young man from Matt's visions, at a [séance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Séance "Séance"), emitting [ectoplasm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ectoplasm_\(paranormal\) "Ectoplasm (paranormal)") from his mouth. They also find a container of desiccated human [eyelids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyelid "Eyelid"). Wendy and Matt discover that the funeral home was run by a man named Ramsey Aickman, who conducted psychic research and would host séances with Jonah acting as a [medium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediumship "Mediumship"). At one séance, all those attending, including Aickman, were found dead, and Jonah disappeared.

Nicholas theorizes that Aickman was practicing [necromancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Necromancy "Necromancy") in an attempt to control the dead and bind them to the house. That night, Nicholas finds human remains in the house and removes them. Matt awakens to find Aickman's symbols carved into his skin. He is taken to the hospital, where he encounters Jonah's ghost. Nicholas and Matt begin to have simultaneous visions revealing Jonah's fate: During the séance, a demonic presence burnt all the attendees in a flash of light. Jonah fled, using a [dumbwaiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dumbwaiter "Dumbwaiter") to escape the basement, but inadvertently became trapped in the [crematory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crematory "Crematory"), where he was [cremated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cremation "Cremation") alive.

Peter and Sara learn that Matt's cancer treatments have had no effect. They then discover that Matt has escaped the hospital. At home, Nicholas leaves a message telling the family to get out immediately, as it was Jonah's spirit that protected them. Matt breaks through the walls in the front room with an axe, revealing the dusty corpses Aickman hid in the walls. He forces Wendy and the children outside before barricading himself in the house and tearing down the other walls as corpses begin to tumble into the room. Jonah seemingly [possesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirit_possession "Spirit possession") Matt, who lights the bodies and the room on fire. Later on, investigators arrive at the house only to find it engulfed in flames.

As the fire department arrives, Sara and Peter frantically try to get in to save Matt. The spirits, finally freed, disappear. Outside, everyone watches tearfully as the emergency crew attempts to revive a dying Matt. As Matt slips away, he experiences a vision of himself standing in the graveyard where he sees Jonah, no longer appearing burnt. He seems about to follow Jonah when he hears his mother's voice. Matt returns to his body, and Jonah's spirit leaves him.

An [intertitle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intertitle "Intertitle") reveals that after the events, Matt's cancer miraculously disappeared. The house was rebuilt and resold with no further reported incidents of haunting.

## Production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")\]

### Development

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Development")\]

The origins of *The Haunting in Connecticut* date back to 2003, when screenwriter and producer [Daniel Farrands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Farrands "Daniel Farrands") presented the story to producer [Andrew Trapani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Trapani "Andrew Trapani").[\[17\]](#cite_note-TwoDeadBoys-19)[\[18\]](#cite_note-20) The film's screenplay, by [Adam Simon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Simon "Adam Simon") and Tim Metcalfe, is based on the alleged supernatural experiences of Carmen Snedeker and her family, who moved into a former [Southington, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southington,_Connecticut "Southington, Connecticut") funeral home during her son Stephen's cancer treatments in 1986\.[\[19\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWetmore202132-21)[\[20\]](#cite_note-22) The Snedekers' experiences were documented in the 1992 book *In a Dark Place: The Story of a True Haunting* by [Ray Garton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Garton "Ray Garton").[\[19\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWetmore202132-21) Carmen Snedeker provided input to the screenwriters over the course of approximately two years while the screenplay was being drafted.[\[21\]](#cite_note-Morrow-23)

In early 2007, [Gold Circle Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Circle_Films "Gold Circle Films") was reportedly discussing a directing contract with [John Carpenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carpenter "John Carpenter") for *The Haunting in Connecticut*. Although Carpenter was initially interested, the deal quickly fell through due to creative differences. Carpenter did enjoy the film's concept and would later agree to direct *[The Ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ward_\(film\) "The Ward (film)")* due to its similarities in tone and theme with *The Haunting in Connecticut*.[\[22\]](#cite_note-24)

### Casting

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Casting")\]

Virginia Madsen was cast in the film in May 2007 as Sara Campbell, the matriarch of the family.[\[23\]](#cite_note-25) According to producer [Paul Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Brooks "Paul Brooks"), Madsen was the first actress sought for the role.[\[17\]](#cite_note-TwoDeadBoys-19) "Virginia had a great combination of warmth and authority," said director Cornwell, "and she really helped to sell the reality of the family’s experience."[\[24\]](#cite_note-StuffWeLike-26)

Madsen stated that she had been interested in making a horror film, and had recently read "about 25 scripts" that she felt gave her "nothing to do."[\[17\]](#cite_note-TwoDeadBoys-19) When the role was offered to her, Madsen responded positively to the screenplay and its elements of interpersonal family drama.[\[17\]](#cite_note-TwoDeadBoys-19) Commenting on her portrayal of a real person, Madsen said: "I think something life-changing happened to that family. I don't know how much of what happened would meet my definition of real. I don't know what happened to them—and I don't even know how much I believe. Then, of course, we took a little Hollywood license. In the end, I can only play what's in the script."[\[21\]](#cite_note-Morrow-23)

In September 2007, *[The Hollywood Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hollywood_Reporter "The Hollywood Reporter")* announced the casting of Kyle Gallner, Martin Donovan, and Elias Koteas.[\[25\]](#cite_note-27) The film reunited Madsen and Koteas, who had previously been co-stars in the horror film *[The Prophecy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Prophecy "The Prophecy")* (1995).[\[26\]](#cite_note-King-28)

### Filming

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Filming")\]

[Principal photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_photography "Principal photography") began on September 10, 2007, in [Teulon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teulon "Teulon") and [Winnipeg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winnipeg "Winnipeg"), Manitoba Canada,[\[27\]](#cite_note-29) and was completed after approximately two months.[\[21\]](#cite_note-Morrow-23) The majority of filming took place in a historic 101-year-old home in Teulon.[\[26\]](#cite_note-King-28)

The film features several historical photographs from the archives of [Thomas Glendenning Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Glendenning_Hamilton "Thomas Glendenning Hamilton"), a Canadian [spiritualist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritualism_\(movement\) "Spiritualism (movement)") who photographed numerous séances, depicting alleged incidents of ectoplasm and other supernatural phenomena.[\[28\]](#cite_note-30)

## Factual basis

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Factual basis")\]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Lorraine_Warren.jpg/250px-Lorraine_Warren.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lorraine_Warren.jpg)

[Lorraine Warren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_and_Lorraine_Warren "Ed and Lorraine Warren"), who investigated the alleged haunting depicted in the film, indicated the film was "very loosely based" on the actual investigation[\[29\]](#cite_note-Reel-31)

Promotional material for the film claimed that it was "based on true events" experienced by the Snedeker family of Southington, Connecticut, in 1986\.[\[30\]](#cite_note-Radford-32) Paranormal investigators [Ed and Lorraine Warren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_and_Lorraine_Warren "Ed and Lorraine Warren") claimed that the Snedeker house was a former funeral home where morticians regularly practiced [necromancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Necromancy "Necromancy") and engaged in [necrophilia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Necrophilia "Necrophilia"), and that there were "powerful" supernatural "forces at work" that were cured by an [exorcism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exorcism "Exorcism").[\[30\]](#cite_note-Radford-32)[\[29\]](#cite_note-Reel-31)[\[31\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrown20087-33) Carmen Snedeker's claims of haunting by an "evil entity" and subsequent exorcism were dramatized in episodes of the television series *[A Haunting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Haunting "A Haunting")* (2002),[\[32\]](#cite_note-34) *[Paranormal Witness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paranormal_Witness "Paranormal Witness")* (2012),[\[33\]](#cite_note-35) and *[Mysteries at the Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mysteries_at_the_Museum "Mysteries at the Museum")* (2014).[\[34\]](#cite_note-36)[\[35\]](#cite_note-37)

However, according to skeptical investigator [Benjamin Radford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Radford "Benjamin Radford"), there is "little or no proof that anything supernatural occurred at the house."[\[36\]](#cite_note-livescience.com-38) Radford wrote that author [Ray Garton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Garton "Ray Garton") was employed by the Warrens to write the supposedly "true story" and was instructed by Ed Warren, "You've got some of the story — just use what works and make the rest up… Just make it up and make it scary."[\[36\]](#cite_note-livescience.com-38)

Researcher [Joe Nickell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Nickell "Joe Nickell") has dismissed the story as a [hoax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoax "Hoax"),[\[37\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENickell2012286-39) and claimed that the Snedekers' landlady "found the whole story ridiculous," adding that no residents before or since had experienced anything unusual in the home.[\[36\]](#cite_note-livescience.com-38) The landlady also noted that, despite their claims of paranormal activity, the Snedekers continued to reside in the home for over two years before deciding to leave.[\[36\]](#cite_note-livescience.com-38) Nickell noted that since Ed Warren died in 2006, some of his coauthors have admitted he "told them to make up incidents and details to create scary stories."[\[37\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENickell2012286-39) In an interview prior to the film's release, Lorraine Warren commented:

> The movie is very, very loosely based on the actual investigation... It was back in the '80s. We were called, it was very late at night, that Ed and I were called by a woman and her niece who were living with her at the time... The boys were the first to start talking about things they had seen and experienced, saying they were terrified. The parents were kind of chastising the kids—they thought it was all crazy. But the kids were so scared they started sleeping on the floor in the living room. It finally got to the point where we contacted the bishop’s office in [Hartford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartford,_Connecticut "Hartford, Connecticut"). Thank God he was very open to our work and what was going on. He sent two priests to the house and both of these priests were very high in the church. One had been used as an exorcist. They came to the house and said mass.[\[29\]](#cite_note-Reel-31)

## Release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Release")\]

In October 2008, [MTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV "MTV") released the film's first official theatrical trailer.[\[38\]](#cite_note-40) The film was originally planned for a June 19, 2009 theatrical release,[\[39\]](#cite_note-41) but in February 2009, its distributor, [Lionsgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionsgate_Films "Lionsgate Films"), announced that the release had been moved to March of that year.[\[40\]](#cite_note-42)

*The Haunting in Connecticut* premiered at [South by Southwest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_by_Southwest "South by Southwest") in [Austin, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin,_Texas "Austin, Texas") on March 17, 2009\.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Leydon-1)[\[41\]](#cite_note-43) It was theatrically released in the United States and Canada ten days later, on March 27, 2009\.[\[42\]](#cite_note-44) Lionsgate handled distribution in the United States, while in Canada, the film was distributed by [Maple Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maple_Pictures "Maple Pictures").[\[43\]](#cite_note-45) Due to favorable [test screenings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Test_screening "Test screening"), Lionsgate increased the film's U.S. release platform from approximately 2,200 screens to over 2,700.[\[44\]](#cite_note-46)

The owners of the actual Southington, Connecticut home depicted in the film reported that the film's publicity had resulted in numerous individuals visiting and photographing the residence in the weeks leading up to its release.[\[45\]](#cite_note-47)

### Home media

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Home media")\]

*The Haunting in Connecticut* was released on [DVD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DVD "DVD") and [Blu-ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blu-ray "Blu-ray") on July 14, 2009, featuring an extended 102-minute cut of the film.[\[3\]](#cite_note-McGaughy-3)[\[46\]](#cite_note-Gingold-48)[\[47\]](#cite_note-49) It debuted in the number one position on the DVD and Blu-ray charts with 1\.5 million units sold.[\[48\]](#cite_note-50) [Rentrak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rentrak "Rentrak") reported that the DVD release of *The Haunting in Connecticut* was no. 1 in DVD sales for the week ending July 19, 2009\.[\[49\]](#cite_note-51)[\[50\]](#cite_note-52)[\[51\]](#cite_note-53)

The extended version DVD includes a commentary with director Peter Cornwell, co-writer Adam Simon, producer [Andrew Trapani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Trapani "Andrew Trapani"), and editor Tom Elkins, a second commentary with the director and actors Virginia Madsen and Kyle Gallner, [deleted scenes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deleted_scene "Deleted scene") with optional director commentary, featurettes ("Two Dead Boys: Making of The Haunting in Connecticut", "The Fear is Real: Re-Investigating the Haunting", "Memento Mori: The History of Post Mortem Photography", "Anatomy of a Haunting"), and a digital copy of the film on a second disc.[\[46\]](#cite_note-Gingold-48)

The DVD material was produced and directed by Daniel Farrands, who also served as a producer on the film. "Anatomy of a Haunting" featured commentary by parapsychological researchers Dr. Barry E. Taff and Jack Rourke.[\[52\]](#cite_note-54) The DVD and Blu-ray release of *The Haunting in Connecticut* was the recipient of the *Best Ghost Story* award in *[Home Media Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Media_Magazine "Home Media Magazine")*'s 2009 Reaper Awards ceremony held in Los Angeles in October 2009\.[\[53\]](#cite_note-Latchem-55)

## Reception

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Reception")\]

### Box office

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Box office")\]

In North America, the film opened in second place (behind *[Monsters vs. Aliens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monsters_vs._Aliens "Monsters vs. Aliens")*), averaging $8,420 at 2,732 theatres and grossing $23,004,765.[\[6\]](#cite_note-BOM-7)[\[54\]](#cite_note-56) *[The Hollywood Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hollywood_Reporter "The Hollywood Reporter")* noted the film was a financial success, reporting in June 2009 that it was the 25th-most profitable film of the year at that time.[\[55\]](#cite_note-Zeitchik-57)

The film remained in distribution in 39 international markets through July 22, 2010\.[\[6\]](#cite_note-BOM-7) Its final North American gross was $55.4 million and it made a further $23.4 million internationally for a worldwide total of $78.8 million.[\[7\]](#cite_note-NUM-8) In 2012, the film was re-released in [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"), where it grossed an additional $41,961.[\[6\]](#cite_note-BOM-7)

### Critical response

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Haunting_in_Connecticut&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Critical response")\]

On the [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), 17% of 105 critics' reviews are positive, with an average rating of 4\.3/10. The website's consensus reads: "Though it features a few scares and some creepy atmosphere, *The Haunting in Connecticut* ultimately relies too much on familiar horror cliches to achieve its goals."[\[56\]](#cite_note-Rotten_Tomatoes-58) [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), which uses a [weighted average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_arithmetic_mean "Weighted arithmetic mean"), assigned the film a score of 33 out of 100, based on 23 critics, indicating "generally unfavorable" reviews.[\[57\]](#cite_note-Metacritic-59) Audiences polled by [CinemaScore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CinemaScore "CinemaScore") gave the film an average grade of "B−" on an A+ to F scale.[\[58\]](#cite_note-60) While the film was mainly criticized for its use of horror cliches and "jump" scare tactics,[\[59\]](#cite_note-61) certain aspects of the film were praised by many critics, including the atmosphere and performances.[\[ii\]](#cite_note-reviews-17)

Jeannette Catsoulis of *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* praised the film's "genuinely grisly imagery" but expressed dislike for its "screechy" musical score, summarizing: "Spinning another based-on-actual-events tale of a family ejected from its home by angry spirits, *The Haunting in Connecticut* gives you the creeps, the giggles and the groans in almost equal measure."[\[60\]](#cite_note-62) [Alonso Duralde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alonso_Duralde "Alonso Duralde") of *[Today](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Today_\(American_TV_program\) "Today (American TV program)")* found the film's use of jump scares "gimmicky," adding that he wished the film "had trusted its plot and its dank visuals—which are often extraordinary—instead of relying on cheap thrills of the cat-jumps-out-of-the-closet variety."[\[11\]](#cite_note-Duralde-12) Film critic [Roger Ebert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Ebert "Roger Ebert") said the film "is a technically proficient horror movie and well acted," though he gave the movie only two stars.[\[61\]](#cite_note-63) Writing for *[Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_\(magazine\) "Empire (magazine)")*, [Kim Newman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Newman "Kim Newman") awarded the film two out of five stars, writing: "There’s a germ of an idea in the terminally ill teen attuned to seeing ghosts because he’s almost one himself, but Gallner’s smothered by Madsen’s hand-wringing mom, Martin Donovan’s dad and smarmy Elias Koteas in an *[Exorcist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Exorcist "The Exorcist")* hat. It has gruesome touches (a box of snipped-off eyelids), but the sudden-grab scares soon get pretty tiresome."[\[62\]](#cite_note-64)

Jim Vejvoda of *[IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN "IGN")* found the film "effective" despite being formulaic, adding that it "has very human and relatable characters at its core—a family that was already in peril due to the terminal illness of a family member—that keeps the viewer engaged in the story even as things grow more fantastical."[\[12\]](#cite_note-Vejvoda-13) Katherine Monk of the *[Calgary Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calgary_Herald "Calgary Herald")* similarly praised the film's emotional core, writing: "Like all movies crafted in the twilight world between the dead and the living, *The Haunting in Connecticut* ramps up suspense by pulling these two dimensions as close together as possible—with Matt becoming the human junction point."[\[63\]](#cite_note-65)

[Joe Leydon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Leydon "Joe Leydon") of *[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_\(magazine\) "Variety (magazine)")* noted that director Cornwell "sets up the story with brisk efficiency and a reasonable degree of logic," but ultimately felt that "nothing here rises above the level of routine haunted-house bumping-in-the-night."[\[1\]](#cite_note-Leydon-1) Writing for the *[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times "Los Angeles Times")*, Mark Olsen observed that the film "seems most at ease when it is playing more like a domestic drama than a horror tale, with the rather unsettling implication early on that what is happening may be a hallucinatory side effect of the boy’s trial cancer treatments. But *Haunting* suffers for its need to be sold as a straight-up horror film, and the fact it has been seemingly retrofitted as such."[\[64\]](#cite_note-66)

Tim Robey of *[The Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Daily_Telegraph "The Daily Telegraph")* gave the film a favorable review, writing: "The movie's heebie-jeebie sound design errs on the side of shameless, but there's a strong emotional core here, and a pretty good script... This is the best \[haunted house film\] in quite a while."[\[13\]](#cite_note-Robey-14) Randall King of the *[Winnipeg Free Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winnipeg_Free_Press "Winnipeg Free Press")* praised the cast as "sufficiently skilled" and found the atmosphere and filming locations effective.[\[65\]](#cite_note-KingReview-67) Sara Schieron of *[Boxoffice Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxoffice_Pro "Boxoffice Pro")* awarded the film three out of five stars, summarizing: "For as flawed as it is, *Haunting* features too many good bits to disregard... For an odd little relic—or should I say throwback?—the film’s scary parts certainly stick to you. You may laugh at the dramatics but you’ll be afraid to turn the light off when you go to bed."[\[66\]](#cite_note-68)

While production of *A Haunting in New York* never materialized, Gold Circle Films produced a [spiritual successor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_successor "Spiritual successor") sequel, *[The Haunting in Connecticut 2: Ghosts of Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Haunting_in_Connecticut_2:_Ghosts_of_Georgia "The Haunting in Connecticut 2: Ghosts of Georgia")*.[\[55\]](#cite_note-Zeitchik-57) [Ti West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ti_West "Ti West") was originally attached to direct,[\[55\]](#cite_note-Zeitchik-57) though Tom Elkins was ultimately hired as director, with David Coggeshall as the screenwriter.[\[70\]](#cite_note-72)[\[71\]](#cite_note-73)[\[72\]](#cite_note-74) It was released in a limited theatrical run, and through [video on demand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_on_demand "Video on demand"), on February 1, 2013\.[\[73\]](#cite_note-75)

All the evidence converges on one answer. Here's my analysis summary:

**Barcode structure (1000 stripes ≈ 5.5 s each for a 92-min film):**
1. **Extremely dark overall** — mean luminance ~28/255 (11%), the darkest possible profile among the candidates; warm desaturated sepia-brown house interiors with occasional steel-blue night/hospital bands — exactly the "dank visuals" critics described for *The Haunting in Connecticut*, a horror film shot almost entirely inside a dark former funeral home.
2. **A ~4-minute wall of saturated fire-orange at 85.4–89.4%** (≈78–82 min), peaking at RGB (83, 41, 9) — the climax where Matt/Jonah lights the corpses in the walls and the house is found "engulfed in flames."
3. **A bright neutral white flash at 90.5%** (RGB ≈ 102,104,100) — the "flash of light" / graveyard vision / floodlit revival scene.
4. **Pure neutral-gray bands (R=G=B exactly) at 92.5–95%** — white text on black: the film's famous intertitle ("Matt's cancer miraculously disappeared...") followed by credits, then pure black.

None of the other candidates fit: *I, Frankenstein* is cool blue-toned; *Knight of Cups* (Malick) and *Midnight Sun* are bright/colorful; *Draft Day*, *Brain on Fire*, *American Animals*, *Puncture*, *99 Homes*, *Detachment* are daytime dramas with no extended fire climax or white-on-black intertitle ending.

**Answer: F**
